title: Krishnamoorthi Wins 256 Cosponsors for July Indian American Heritage Month Resolution
excerpt: The Illinois Democrat's bipartisan resolution ties a July heritage month to the 1946 Luce-Celler Act, which first opened U.S. citizenship to people of Indian descent.
body:
• Rep. Raja Krishnamoorthi (D-IL) introduced a bipartisan House resolution with 256 cosponsors supporting the designation of July as Indian American Heritage Month.
  • July was chosen to commemorate the Luce-Celler Act, signed on July 2, 1946, which first made people of Indian descent eligible for U.S. naturalization.
  • The resolution cites more than 5.2 million Indian Americans and their contributions across medicine, technology, business, public service, the military, education and the arts.
  • For readers: a House resolution is an expression of the House's position, not a law or a federal holiday — July observances would be marked by schools, cities and community groups, with the resolution text posted on Krishnamoorthi's House.gov page.

Rep. Raja Krishnamoorthi of Illinois has introduced a bipartisan resolution in the U.S. House of Representatives, backed by 256 cosponsors, that supports designating July as Indian American Heritage Month. The resolution, announced in a statement on his House.gov page, honors generations of Indian American contributions to the United States and the community's religious and cultural diversity.

With 256 cosponsors in a 435-member chamber, the measure starts with the support of a majority of the House — an unusually broad base for a heritage designation, and one that spans both parties.

"Indian Americans have helped shape this country for generations, from breakthroughs that have saved lives and businesses that have created jobs to lifetimes of service in our military and public office."

— Rep. Raja Krishnamoorthi (D-IL)

Why July

The choice of July is tied to a specific date in immigration history. On July 2, 1946, President Harry S. Truman signed the Luce-Celler Act, which made people of Indian descent eligible for naturalization as American citizens for the first time in decades. Before that law, Indian immigrants faced the same exclusion regime that had barred most Asian immigration since the early twentieth century.

The resolution frames July as a month to recognize what followed that opening: a community that now numbers more than 5.2 million people, according to the statement, with contributions the text lists across science and medicine, technology and business, public service and the military, education and philanthropy, arts and culture, and athletics.

A wider bipartisan track in Congress

Krishnamoorthi's resolution is the largest of several recent bipartisan efforts to put Indian American recognition on the congressional record. Rep. Tom Suozzi (D-NY) and Rep. Young Kim (R-CA) recently led a separate Bipartisan Indian American Heritage Resolution, carried in a Suozzi press release via LegiStorm, that recognizes Indian American accomplishments and condemns hate, discrimination and violence against Indian Americans and the broader South Asian community, including people targeted for Hindu, Sikh, Jain, Muslim or other religious or cultural identity.

"Indian Americans are an integral part of our community in Southern California and across the United States," Rep. Kim said in that release. "Their success stories reflect the very best of the American Dream."

What it means for the community

A heritage-month designation does not create a federal holiday, change immigration law or fund programs. Its practical effect is recognition: it gives schools, libraries, city councils and employers a congressional reference point for scheduling Indian American history and culture programming each July, in the same way other heritage months structure programming through the year.

For Indian American families, the date also carries a specific teaching point. The Luce-Celler anniversary marks the moment Indian immigrants could first become citizens in the modern era — 80 years before the community reached its current size and presence in Congress itself, where Krishnamoorthi is one of a small group of Indian American lawmakers.

What happens next

The resolution has been introduced and its full text is linked from Krishnamoorthi's House page. Heritage resolutions typically move by referral to committee and, when they advance, by adoption on the House floor rather than through the full legislative process required for bills. With 256 cosponsors already signed on, the measure begins that process with majority support in the chamber. If adopted, the first July marked under the designation would be July 2027.
